meta.title: Information Technology Act, 2000 — Key Sections Reference
meta.note: Educational plain-language summaries. NOT legal advice and not the authoritative text. Always consult the bare Act and current amendments.
meta.source_hint: Refer to the official IT Act, 2000 (as amended by the IT (Amendment) Act, 2008) and the IT Rules, 2021.

sections.title: Penalty and compensation for damage to computer, computer system, etc.
sections.summary: Covers unauthorised access, downloading, introducing viruses, causing damage, disrupting, denying access, or tampering with a computer, computer system or network without the owner's permission. The person is liable to pay damages by way of compensation to the affected party.
sections.penalty: Liable to pay damages by way of compensation to the person affected. No upper cap fixed in the section after the 2008 amendment.

sections.title: Compensation for failure to protect data
sections.summary: A body corporate that possesses, deals with or handles sensitive personal data in a computer resource it owns or operates, and is negligent in implementing and maintaining reasonable security practices, causing wrongful loss or gain, is liable to pay compensation to the affected person.
sections.penalty: Liable to pay damages by way of compensation to the affected person. Amount determined on the facts; no statutory ceiling.

sections.title: Tampering with computer source documents
sections.summary: Knowingly or intentionally concealing, destroying or altering (or causing another to conceal, destroy or alter) computer source code required to be kept or maintained by law.
sections.penalty: Imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine up to Rs. 2 lakh, or both.

sections.title: Computer related offences
sections.summary: If any act referred to in Section 43 is done dishonestly or fraudulently, it becomes a criminal offence under Section 66 (e.g., dishonest hacking, data theft, denial of service).
sections.penalty: Imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine up to Rs. 5 lakh, or both.

sections.title: Punishment for identity theft
sections.summary: Fraudulently or dishonestly using another person's electronic signature, password or any other unique identification feature (identity theft).
sections.penalty: Imprisonment up to 3 years and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh.

sections.title: Cheating by personation using computer resource
sections.summary: Cheating by personation (pretending to be someone else) by means of any communication device or computer resource — the legal basis for many phishing, vishing and online-fraud cases.
sections.penalty: Imprisonment up to 3 years and fine up to Rs. 1 lakh.

sections.title: Punishment for violation of privacy
sections.summary: Intentionally capturing, publishing or transmitting the image of a private area of any person without consent, under circumstances violating that person's privacy.
sections.penalty: Imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine up to Rs. 2 lakh, or both.

sections.title: Punishment for cyber terrorism
sections.summary: Acts intended to threaten the unity, integrity, security or sovereignty of India, or to strike terror, by denying access to a computer resource, unauthorised access to protected systems, or introducing contaminants — and acts causing or likely to cause death, injury, damage to critical infrastructure, or access to restricted information affecting national security.
sections.penalty: Imprisonment which may extend to imprisonment for life.

sections.title: Publishing or transmitting obscene material in electronic form
sections.summary: Publishing or transmitting, in electronic form, material that is lascivious or appeals to prurient interest, or tends to deprave and corrupt those likely to read, see or hear it. (Sections 67A and 67B deal with sexually explicit material and child sexual abuse material respectively, with higher penalties.)
sections.penalty: First conviction: imprisonment up to 3 years and fine up to Rs. 5 lakh. Subsequent conviction: up to 5 years and fine up to Rs. 10 lakh.

sections.title: Power to issue directions for interception, monitoring or decryption
sections.summary: Empowers the Central or State Government to direct interception, monitoring or decryption of information through any computer resource, in the interest of the sovereignty and integrity of India, defence, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, or for preventing incitement to a cognizable offence. A subscriber/intermediary failing to assist may be punished.
sections.penalty: Failure to assist the agency: imprisonment up to 7 years and fine (for the intermediary/person who fails to comply).

sections.title: Power to block public access to information
sections.summary: Empowers the Central Government to direct any agency or intermediary to block public access to information through a computer resource, on the grounds of sovereignty and integrity of India, defence, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, or preventing incitement to a cognizable offence. The procedure and safeguards are set out in the IT (Blocking) Rules, 2009, which include a Committee and review mechanism.
sections.penalty: An intermediary that fails to comply with a blocking direction: imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.

sections.title: Protected system
sections.summary: The appropriate Government may declare any computer resource which directly or indirectly affects a Critical Information Infrastructure to be a 'protected system'. Unauthorised access to a protected system is a serious offence.
sections.penalty: Unauthorised access to a protected system: imprisonment up to 10 years and fine.

sections.title: Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In)
sections.summary: Designates CERT-In as the national agency for incident response — collecting, analysing and disseminating information on cyber incidents, issuing alerts and advisories, coordinating emergency response, and issuing directions. Service providers, intermediaries, data centres and body corporates must comply with CERT-In directions (including the 2022 incident-reporting directions).
sections.penalty: Failure to provide information or comply with CERT-In directions: imprisonment up to 1 year, or fine up to Rs. 1 lakh, or both.

sections.title: Exemption from liability of intermediary (safe harbour)
sections.summary: Provides conditional 'safe harbour' — an intermediary is not liable for third-party information it hosts if it is a mere conduit, observes due diligence, and does not initiate/select/modify the transmission. Protection is lost if the intermediary conspires/abets or fails to expeditiously remove content on actual knowledge or on being notified by the appropriate Government/agency. Due-diligence obligations are detailed in the IT Rules, 2021.
sections.penalty: No direct penalty; loss of safe-harbour exposes the intermediary to liability for the underlying content.

rules_2021.title: Intermediary Guidelines & Digital Media Ethics Code Rules, 2021
rules_2021.summary: Framed under the IT Act, 2000 (mainly ss. 79 and 87). Part II prescribes due-diligence obligations for intermediaries; Part III (administered by the Ministry of I&B) covers a Code of Ethics and grievance mechanism for digital news publishers and OTT platforms.
rules_2021.penalty: Non-compliance can lead to loss of safe harbour under Section 79 and consequent liability.

rules_2021.title: Publish rules, privacy policy and user agreement; inform users of prohibited content
rules_2021.summary: Intermediaries must prominently publish their rules, privacy policy and user agreement, and make reasonable efforts to cause users not to host or share specified categories of unlawful/prohibited content.
rules_2021.penalty: Failure affects the intermediary's Section 79 safe harbour.

rules_2021.title: Takedown on actual knowledge / court order or government notification
rules_2021.summary: On receiving actual knowledge via a court order or a notification from the appropriate Government/agency, an intermediary must not host/store/publish the unlawful information and must remove or disable access to it within 36 hours.
rules_2021.penalty: Failure affects Section 79 safe harbour and can attract liability.

rules_2021.title: Grievance redressal — acknowledge 24h, resolve 15 days; 24h for certain content
rules_2021.summary: Intermediaries must appoint a Grievance Officer, acknowledge complaints within 24 hours and dispose of them within 15 days. Complaints about certain content (e.g., non-consensual intimate imagery) must be actioned within 24 hours.

rules_2021.title: Additional due diligence for Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs)
rules_2021.summary: SSMIs (above a notified user threshold) must appoint a Chief Compliance Officer, a Nodal Contact Person and a resident Grievance Officer (all in India), publish monthly compliance reports, and — for messaging services — enable identification of the first originator of information where lawfully required.
rules_2021.penalty: Non-compliance can lead to loss of safe harbour under Section 79.

rules_2021.title: Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC)
rules_2021.summary: Introduced by the 2022 amendment: users dissatisfied with an intermediary's grievance decision may appeal to a Grievance Appellate Committee within 30 days, providing an appellate layer above the intermediary's own Grievance Officer.
rules_2021.penalty: Applies to intermediary grievance decisions; supports Section 79 compliance framework.
